identification.title: The Old Rugged Cross
identification.notes: Words and music by George Bennard (1873-1958), an American evangelist converted in the Salvation Army and later Methodist. Wikipedia dates the hymn to 1912 and notes that Bennard himself gave 1913; it was first performed complete in 1913 and published in 1915. He is said to have begun the first verse in Albion, Michigan, in 1912 and finished it at Sturgeon Bay, Wisconsin; Charles Gabriel helped with the harmony. Homer Rodeheaver bought the rights and popularised it in Billy Sunday's campaigns. Public domain in the United States. The slug is kept. Reviewed as the text, not as any one recording.

claims.structuralNotes: Four stanzas, each followed by a refrain. The first stanza sets the cross as an emblem of shame that the singer nonetheless loves, because the Son died there for sinners. The second speaks of its strange attraction. The third tells of the blood-stained cross where Christ suffered, pardoning and sanctifying. The fourth turns to the singer's commitment to bear shame and look for the heavenly crown. The refrain pledges to cherish and cling to the cross and to exchange it for a crown. The voice is first-person devotion that narrates Calvary and then vows loyalty.

strengths.title: The cross at the centre
strengths.explanation: Every stanza returns to Calvary, and the first and third state that Christ died there for sinners and that his blood pardons and sanctifies.
strengths.scriptureRationale: The word of the cross as the power of God - the hymn's centre.

strengths.title: Pardon through his blood
strengths.explanation: The third stanza connects Christ's suffering and blood to pardon and cleansing, so the singer's standing rests on what he did.
strengths.scriptureRationale: Christ put forward as a propitiation by his blood.

strengths.title: Taking up the cross
strengths.explanation: The fourth stanza answers the cross with willingness to bear reproach, in the sense of the call to take up the cross daily.
strengths.scriptureRationale: If anyone would come after me, let him take up his cross daily.

strengths.title: The crown at the end
strengths.explanation: The crown language looks to the reward promised to the faithful.
strengths.scriptureRationale: The crown of righteousness laid up for those who love his appearing.

doctrinesAffirmed: Pardon and sanctification through his blood
The shame and glory of the cross
theological.assessment: Nothing to correct on the reading note. The cross is at the centre, and the crown language is biblical. The refrain is the singer's own pledge, so the voice is testimonial rather than credal. No independent assessment of its teaching was loaded for this review, so this is a clean record from the text alone.

strengths.title: Familiar waltz-time melody
strengths.explanation: The note describes an extremely familiar waltz-time tune that is easy to sing, with a refrain after each stanza.

strengths.title: Suited to Lent and Good Friday
strengths.explanation: Its cross-centred content fits Lent, Good Friday and the Lord's Supper.

range.note: No chart was read for this review, so the pitches are not stated.

communal.repetitionAssessment: The refrain returns after each stanza and gathers each telling of Calvary into the same pledge, so the repetition carries the song's point.
communal.assessment: Congregational in form: four stanzas and a refrain in waltz time, familiar to many rooms.

strengths.title: The Son and the cross are named
strengths.explanation: The song speaks of the Son who died on the cross for sinners, so its subject is plain.

clarity.assessment: Clear. Cross and crown are scriptural images, and nothing in the song is open to a wrong reading.

synthesis.summary: A hymn by George Bennard, first performed complete in 1913 and published in 1915, in four stanzas with a refrain. It puts the cross at the centre: Christ died there for sinners, his blood pardons and sanctifies, and the singer pledges to bear reproach and wait for the heavenly crown. The voice is the singer's own devotion. No independent source assessing its teaching was loaded.
